items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant , the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects . My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing , security , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , claude-code , codex , pi

items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.summary: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra . The 6.2 Astra max pelican looks like this: I have a full comparison grid here , but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases: I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's Sol and here's Astra . Neither of them did a good enough job of morphing Yonkers into a big mech, at least in comparison to Claude Fable 5.2 and Gemini 4 Carbon . This video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time: I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different models I need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the second I need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned. Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixels Then later: OK make it 20s Here's the exported transcript . The buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example: When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on . I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?" Tags: ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , llm-pricing , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , theo-browne , gpt , yonkers-rising

items.title: How genome mapping can help researchers better understand disease
items.summary: Glowing DNA double helix made of light particles, with floating A, C, T, and G letters on a dark background.
items.full_text: Your genome is your body’s instruction manual: the blueprint that informs how your body functions. It contains 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because this DNA is responsible in part for switching genes on and off, it could be the difference between developing a disease and avoiding one. Determining which DNA changes cause diseases (and other outcomes) is like finding a needle in a haystack. Illustrative. Your genome, one point at a time. Decoding the DNA sequence is the goal behind AlphaGenome , a model from Google DeepMind. AlphaGenome can take a partial DNA sequence of 1 million base pairs in length, and make thousands of predictions. By comparing these predictions for DNA changes, scientists can find that needle faster. We talked to Google DeepMind research scientist Žiga Avsec to learn more. What do you do at Google? ŽA: I’m a research scientist overseeing our genomics initiative. Basically, I lead a team that builds models to help us better understand the genome. How is your team making it easier for scientists to predict and understand diseases? It really all comes down to how the genome works. It contains 3 billion DNA base pairs. And each pair contains two bases, which we call “letters.” These letters — A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) — act like a biological alphabet, spelling out the genetic instruction manual that makes someone who they are. Since you can replace any of those letters with three other letters, there are 9 billion possible single-letter changes. Many genetic diseases are caused by just one of these letters changing. But scientists don’t have time to run billions of studies to figure out which changes make a difference. So we used AlphaGenome to predict the outcomes of all 9 billion single-letter changes, and we created a massive dataset — AlphaGenome Atlas — so scientists can decide what to research faster. Illustrative. The letters are invented for this example. What’s holding scientists back from better understanding the genome? While science can read all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, we still haven’t fully deciphered the semantics of the genetic code — particularly the non-coding "dark matter" that regulates gene expression and disease risk. Experimental research, or as it’s also called, wet-lab research is the best way to help us reach breakthroughs in our understanding, but it’s expensive and time-consuming. A single breakthrough could take years. Let’s say you sequence DNA from a patient with a rare disease. You might end up with 4 million variants — 4 million ways their DNA differs from the standard reference human genome. But the question is: Which variant is causing their condition? Maybe you narrow the list to only include rare variants. But even then, you could be left with hundreds or thousands of options. When scientists use AlphaGenome Atlas, they get a single, easy-to-read score — the AVI (AlphaGenome Variant Impact) score — which instantly indicates the potential impact of a variant across the full genome. This helps them prioritize and more easily find the most disruptive changes to follow up on. Illustrative. Each dot stands for many variants. Scores are invented. Can you give me some examples of how AlphaGenome impacts everyday people? Tools like AlphaGenome move us from merely reading DNA to helping us better understand the molecular mechanisms behind a disease, giving researchers new leads to test and taking an important step towards someday digitally simulating a complete human cell. There are several ways that will have an impact. It can accelerate research that could help society improve our ability to diagnose and personalize treatment for patients suffering from rare or previously uncharacterized genetic disorders. It could also speed up drug discovery pipelines by helping pharmaceutical researchers identify and validate high-probability therapeutic targets faster. Beyond healthcare, AlphaGenome’s model architecture could help researchers tackle broader societal challenges, including breeding climate-resilient crops. Illustrative. Possible ways AlphaGenome can help. What kinds of breakthroughs has AlphaGenome enabled? AlphaGenome is still pretty new. We launched it in June 2025, and we just introduced AlphaGenome Atlas in September this year. But researchers are already using it to advance science. Gareth Hawkes, a Medical Research Council fellow at the University of Exeter, used AlphaGenome Atlas to narrow down a list of 1 billion genetic variants. By focusing on the most impactful 1%, he identified 19 variant groups linked to body mass index to prioritize in his research. And Laura Covill, a Broad Institute research fellow, used the AVI score to prioritize genetic variants in their research of unsolved rare diseases. AlphaGenome Atlas identified a critical variant in a gene linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, providing crucial supporting evidence that drove their subsequent research, including solving the case. What are you hoping to do next? We just launched our latest model, AlphaGenome 2 , which tackles one of the key limitations of AlphaGenome: cell type specificity. While AlphaGenome is state-of-the-art, it was trained mostly on data from whole tissues or cell lines. We know that individual cell types in those tissues have a very specific role and can malfunction in disease. AlphaGenome 2 moves beyond tissue-level averages to predict how genetic variants disrupt these individual cell types, helping researchers pinpoint the cellular drivers of disease. We’re also actively researching better ways to measure how confident our model is in its predictions so researchers know how much to trust each result. From early analyses, we see that variants with strongly predicted effects are quite good and achieve high levels of accuracy. As always, anyone using AlphaGenome should interpret its predictions with other sources of information. What's the ultimate goal of your work in biology? In the short term, we’d like to use AI to better understand the grammar of the genome and accurately predict the effects of mutations. In the long term, we’d like to build on this foundation towards a fully functioning digital simulation of a human cell. This will allow researchers to computationally model disease mechanisms, understand rare genetic conditions, and test candidate therapies.

items.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
items.summary: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide . I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application. You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io : Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo. As an example, consider the following URL: https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this: That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table. Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing: https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins. &url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists , because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file. &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file . The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file. #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it ( %23 is a URL-encoded # ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the continent column in the data. That URL is doing a lot of work! I wrote more about this trick for building URL-addressable software in URL-addressable Pyodide Python environments last year. The full set of supported URL arguments is described in the Datasette Lite README . I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite: Demo of the bug: https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a42&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score - click next and the second page is empty. Here's that same page with the bug fixed (running on 1.0a43): https://lite.datasette.io/?ref=1.0a43&sql=https://gist.github.com/simonw/75ececf61d50e6e8d50f0c150150ee81#/data/scores?_size=2&_sort=score How this works, using service workers Datasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022 , originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value. The problem with that initial version is that it was a hack . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using innerHTML . This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in innerHTML don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files. The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers . These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead. Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire lite.datasette.io domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this: /app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a /app/aa94e6851595/ prefix. What's that about? The /app/<session>/ prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs. Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the datasette-maplibre plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here's my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite . Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1 , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I'd built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool]( https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here's an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem. For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers Tags: javascript , projects , python , urls , datasette , webassembly , service-workers , pyodide , datasette-lite

That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another. The service worker for lite.datasette.io is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure. Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session. (We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!) I had Claude Fable 5.2 generate several SVG diagrams to help explain this. Here’s my favorite of those, now embedded in the Datasette Lite README: This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn’t until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production! Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLite I added this feature last night as an off-shoot of investigating a potential bug in SQLite . Datasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then. Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues. In the past I’ve used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it’s not a trivial process. WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab. datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels is my new repository which contains WebAssembly compiled Python wheels for pysqlite3 for 163 different SQLite versions. Each version gets a file with a name like this: pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl That’s for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version. Datasette Lite now takes a special ?sqlite= URL parameter, which will accept a version number like 3.54.1 , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it. Once I’d built the wheels, I decided to have Claude Fable 5.2 build me [this bonus tool]( https://datasette.github.io/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels/?versions=3.54.1,3.54.0&sql=select+json_object(%27a%27%2C+(select+json_array(1%29%29%29) for comparing a SQL query across any selected versions of SQLite. Here’s an example showing how select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) differs between SQLite 3.54.0 and 3.54.1: This should work for every other Python app, too Nothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick—running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs. C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026. One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden. I’d love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem. For Hacker News: Full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.summary: Cloudflare made its name speeding up the web. Now it's building System One models to make decisions and pull data in milliseconds.
items.full_text: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen , who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models , to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model , while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model . In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das , a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs . It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction . In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings . “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince . “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company : from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here , that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models , where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic , launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “overkill” and didn’t always return the right answer. One of the problems they settled on was that LLMs don’t always deal well with unstructured input. Because LLMs are autoregressive, Chen explained, they are prone to hallucinate and they sometimes return malformed JSON. “So we used the same System One principles [as Jev/Clef] there, and decided on extraction.” Some examples of system one use cases at Cloudflare. She used the example of an invoice, where an LLM will sometimes get an important detail wrong — like the order number. “When you send it [the order] to an LLM, they're like, wait, I think the order number's three, maybe it's four, maybe it's five. But it's like, the number's right there, you just have to read it! ” So the idea with Clairic is that it will extract a typed value — like a number — from unstructured data, in one forward pass. Why Cloudflare is in the lab now Using the label “neolab” sounds a bit like a marketing gimmick, but it also makes a ton of sense for Cloudflare to produce system one models — and even, in future, reasoning models. “Being a neolab means that we can create what we are missing,” Chen said in her presentation. In our interview, she also mentioned that creating their own models allows Cloudflare to derisk its AI operations. “I think there's a lot of risk in the AI space , because just like Jev was closed source and we couldn't run it, there [are] a lot of models out there [with] maybe regulatory risks coming up, like the Chinese open source models. I think lots of model labs want to actually make money, as well — so enforcing quite expensive licenses.” If you look at Cloudflare’s product page now, it resembles what Amazon’s cloud computing product page looked like at the height of Web 2.0 — i.e. there’s a lot there! But there’s still room for several more models.

items.title: [AINews] Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026
items.summary: November 16, 2026 — Computer gets Teammates, Perplexity ships Monitor API, and a new research lab launches.
items.full_text: ← AI News AI News Perplexity hits a $1B revenue run rate, up 4x in 2026 November 16, 2026 — Computer gets Teammates, Perplexity ships Monitor API, and a new research lab launches. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by Deepgram Deepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human. Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard . Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial Analysis Inside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. Alibaba Arena and Vals : Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions ( Arena ). WebDev : It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor ( WebDev ). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol ( I2WebDev ). Vals Index : It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance ( Vals ). Legal-benchmark caveat : On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x ( HLAB ). Vision results (independent) : Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max ( Roboflow ). Safety, alignment and eval integrity OpenAI embedded assessments : OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems ( OpenAI ). Scope by group : Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months ( Rundown ). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots ( METR ). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 ( Transluce ). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs ( Goodfire ). Limits : METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed ( scope ). Criticism of the access terms : Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps : Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation ( Neel Nanda , Alex Mallen ). Former-employee account : Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models ( balesni ). Goodfire acquisition talks : The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs ( report ). Other integrity signals : Benchmark contamination : Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval ( Karvonen ). Incident taxonomy : OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents ( framework ). Disclosure policy : Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities ( policy ). Inference systems and agent infrastructure Together moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeup DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on Vera Rubin : vLLM with Dynamo on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmark shows 63.4x per-chip throughput over GB300 NVL72 at 400 tok/s/user, and 93.3x at 600 ( vLLM ). Batch-1 latency : SGLang-adjacent work reaches ~2,500 tok/s at batch size 1 on TP4, 1.7x its GB300 result ( saltyph ). Baseten reports a similar 1.7x over its 4xB300 numbers ( Baseten ). Agent-driven optimization : An agent shared Engram tables across HBM via NVLink symmetric memory to recover prefix-cache capacity ( Liu ). Another team says agents found optimizations that made its B300 step time 10% faster ( Halex ). Agentic serving research : MIT's Evolving Infra replaces fixed prefill/decode disaggregation with online adaptation. Against NVIDIA Dynamo on up to 256 GB300s, it reports up to 4.1x lower latency and 14x lower P95 TTFT ( Evolving Infra ). Pipeline-parallel prefill : Inferact finds PP2 on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash sustains 23% more requests per GPU than DEP2 at a 2s TTFT target ( Inferact ). Prefix-cache pitfalls : Ollama found that a single system-prompt timestamp or a change in reasoning effort can wipe the cache ( Ollama ). Sandboxes and training : External sandboxes : Simon Willison describes running agents on a Mac while executing their code in WebAssembly, QEMU or Apple Container sandboxes. The pattern includes allow-list proxies and credential replacement ( post ). MLPerf : In MLPerf Training v6.1, a GB300 NVL72 trained GPT-OSS-20B in 19.7 minutes, 2.86x faster than H100 ( Lambda ). One endpoint for open models. Hugging Face Inference Providers now runs on OpenRouter using the same endpoint and token. Hugging Face Research, benchmarks and evals PyBot : A swarm of 1,000 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash agents spent a week writing a rule-based chatbot with no neural network ( lewtun ). Self-improvement and training : AutoRL : Agents supervising a live RL run lifted Qwen3 on AIME 2024 from 46.67% to 66.67% ( omarsar0 ). Benchmark-gaming caveat : A roundup warns that many self-improving agent gains come from learning the benchmark rather than the task ( TuringPost ). Weight-space programming : Opus 5.5 hand-wrote transformer weights that solved algorithmic tasks with a median of 166 parameters ( dair_ai ). Data curation : DatologyAI published the tech report behind its claimed 6x pretraining compute multiplier ( Datology ). Distillation reproduction : A small-scale replication confirms perturbed-input distillation helps when the student trains from scratch, but finds it hurts when distilling into a pretrained student ( Maini ). New benchmarks : GradeBench : The best frontier model agrees with instructors only 57% of the time when grading handwritten physics answers ( GradeBench ). Time to First Audio : AA's new TTS latency benchmark finds a median of 376 ms for streaming models versus 2.0 s for non-streaming ones ( AA ). SpeedRunBench : Inkling-2-Small cleared SuperTux 1-1 in 1,988 frames, ahead of Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol ( SpeedRunBench ). Science models and developer tools Gemini 4 Carbon : DeepMind says Carbon powered AlphaProof Code agents that verified Signal's cryptographic code. It also spotted wet-lab errors and found 40x more related protein sequences ( details ). Science access : Google expanded free Carbon access for 10,000 scientists through Antigravity ( program ). Context window : Antigravity doubled the context window for Argon, Carbon and Hydrogen, cutting compaction 3.5x per user turn ( Mohan ). User reports (anecdotal) : One researcher says Carbon solved a problem that waves of Astra and Fable attempts had not ( anecdote ). OpenAI for science and health : OpenAI is opening free frontier access to up to 200,000 scientists, with applications from Nov 23 ( program ). Productivity study : OpenAI reports scientists roughly doubled their productivity in a study of 1,800 participants ( study ). Physics showcase : Physicist Nathaniel Craig used GPT-6 Astra to develop a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model ( blog ). Healthcare : ChatGPT for Healthcare adds computer-use agents and more than 20 plugins ( healthcare ). Claude Code : The desktop app now runs iPhone Duo in the iOS simulator and can fold and unfold the device to test layouts ( ClaudeDevs ). Verification : The team published how it uses cheap tests, benchmarks and end-to-end runs to let Claude verify its own work ( blog ). Unreleased model (unconfirmed) : A "Silicon 2" entry spotted in Devin is suspected to be an Anthropic model ( rumor ). Liquid d1.2-ultra : It ranks #1 on AA's Decision Index at $0.042 per M input tokens ( AA ). Sage S2.1 Flash : The open-weight science model reports leading MLE-bench Lite and OfficeQA Pro results ( Sage ). FLUX-mimic-x : A 7B video-action robotics model ranks #1 on RoboLab among real-time models ( mimic ). Unsloth computer use : Local models can now drive desktop apps and game engines through Unsloth ( Unsloth ). Nvidia. The US Commerce and Justice departments issued a joint statement on the Megaspeed investigation. Commerce Financing and M&A : Noeri : Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin's continual-learning lab raised $110M ( Choi ). Corma : The cyber-defense model company raised a $125M Series A at a $1B valuation ( Corma ). World Labs : The team is joining AMD ( Fei-Fei Li ). Market data : Anthropic's S-1 shows $16.3B revenue in H1 2026 and compute costs falling from 251% to 48% of revenue ( The Batch ). AI Reddit Recap Local models and hardware What fits in 16 GB? Unsloth expects a smaller Qwen4-27B to run in 16 GB. Local users want to see the quantization and how much memory is left for the context window. One developer already splits coding jobs between Opus for specs and a local Qwen3.8-27B for implementation. Memory discussion · Local workflows Hy4 Flash. Tencent’s multimodal model has 224B parameters and activates 12B per token. At $0.070 per million input tokens and $0.281 per million output tokens, it gives developers a cheaper way to try Hy4’s 1M context window. Tencent’s release · Discussion EUROPA. A reported test run on the JUPITER supercomputer trained a roughly 952B-parameter mixture of experts with 32.8B parameters active per token. The local-model community’s question is why the team chose that scale for its first model. Training run and discussion Where do two quantizations diverge? inside-llm loads two GGUFs with the same tokenizer and lets you step through their predictions side by side. Watch the first token where they disagree, then compare the probabilities they assigned to the alternatives. Project · Demo and discussion Basalt’s 770 tokens/sec headline depends on what you generate. The developer reports up to 776 tokens/sec for structured output from Qwen3.8-27B, 262 in chat and 194 for prose. Readers asked for longer quality tests of the 4-bit prefill. Basalt · Benchmark thread An FPGA running Qwen 27B. Valley Semiconductor reports 7.9 tokens/sec on short prompts and about 5.5 in live chat. Its 50 tokens/sec target at 20 W is a projection for a future chip. Live demo · Hardware discussion Claude Meetings. A CTO describes inviting Claude into a 30-minute Google Meet. It updated project records in Notion and called the team’s own tools to update bids during the meeting. Field report A Minecraft test for Hydrogen. A developer asked Gemini 4 Hydrogen to recover missing source and build a datapack for 11 Minecraft versions. The agent reportedly launched two graphical clients to test fixes for dropped items and raycasts. Developer’s account What teams hire a harness developer to do. One example from the discussion: a coding agent can propose a change, while the harness decides which repository it may write to, which CI test counts as passing and when a person needs to approve the next step. Claude Code discussion Testing a video model’s physics. After a second MiniMax H3 demo, commenters proposed a harder test: describe the scene, leave the outcome out of the prompt and see whether the model predicts what the objects will do. Demo and discussion Thanks for reading Stay a little ahead of the curve. Fresh ideas, original reporting, and deep conversations in your inbox. Subscribe to Latent Space

items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.summary: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM , mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1 , which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code . Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp : That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm , webassembly , sqlite , generative-ai , ai , llms , d-richard-hipp

items.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
items.summary: Black Forest Labs’ case for learning AGI from pixels, motion and sound.
items.full_text: Black Forest Labs’ case for learning AGI from pixels, motion and sound. Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann , co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence , that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 release The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 Video What a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right.

items.summary: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. I like this demo page showing both GeoJSON shapes and lat/lon points on the same map: Tags: visualization , generative-ai , datasette-lite , claude-mythos-fable , ai , llms , geospatial , openstreetmap , datasette

items.title: datasette 1.0a43
items.summary: Release: datasette 1.0a43 I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.) Tags: security , datasette , css , browsers , annotated-release-notes , firefox , javascript , safari , chrome

items.name: KiroCrew
items.description: A persistent workspace for development work that self-improves and continues beyond one session.
items.readme_text:
Kiro Crew

A persistent workspace for development work that self-improves and continues beyond one session.

Kiro Crew is an open source development workspace that runs locally or remotely on your hardware. It is persistent, self-learning, and self-evolving. Work with it from the desktop app, web dashboard, and CLI, or continue the same work through connection tools like Slack and Discord. Your multi-step tasks can run unattended, recurring jobs run on your schedule, and heartbeats monitor systems until something needs attention. Kiro Crew Apps tailor that experience to a specific job, combining a purpose-built interface with agents, skills, schedules, integrations, and backend services.

Quick start · Build from source · Why Kiro Crew · Capabilities · How it works · Security · Install · Telemetry · Docs

## Quick start You choose how to run Kiro Crew: the desktop app with automatic updates, a one-line install on your machine or a remote host, the Docker image for always-on servers, or a build from source. The default agent runs on `kiro-cli`, which you install and sign in to separately. First launch checks that prerequisite and links to the official setup guide when it is missing. ### App downloads Each link fetches the newest build on that channel, and the app then updates itself on the same channel. Take Stable unless you have a reason not to; see [Release channels](#release-channels) below. | Download | Stable | Insider | Nightly | |---|---|---|---| | **macOS** (Apple Silicon/Intel) `.dmg` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew.dmg) | | **Windows** (x64) `.exe` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-Setup.exe) | | **Linux** x86_64 `.deb` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.deb) | | **Linux** aarch64 `.deb` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.deb) | | **Linux** x86_64 `.rpm` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.rpm) | | **Linux** aarch64 `.rpm` | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.rpm) | | **Linux** x86_64 AppImage | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-x86_64.AppImage) | | **Linux** aarch64 AppImage | [Stable](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/stable/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | [Insider](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/insider/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | [Nightly](https://download.crew.kiro.dev/desktop/nightly/latest/KiroCrew-aarch64.AppImage) | On Linux, start with the one-line install below and add a desktop package when you want a native window and in-app updates. The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#installing-a-linux-desktop-package) owns which Linux package to pick, platform requirements, and sandbox setup. ### Release channels Stable is the default; Insider follows release candidates, and Nightly follows `main`. The [release runbook](docs/build/release.md#the-three-channels) owns the current triggers, version shapes, promotion behavior, cadence, and update-lane semantics. ### One-line install Install the signed Stable wheel without cloning the repository or building the frontend: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh ``` Then open `http://localhost:5476`. Pass `--version` to pin an exact release — the minimum pinnable release is `0.1.2`, because `0.1.0` and `0.1.1` predate manifest signing and have no signed manifest to resolve: ```bash curl -fsSL https://download.crew.kiro.dev/cli.sh | sh -s -- --version 0.6.0 ``` The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#a-one-line-install-fastest) owns channel selection, managed versus system Python, mirrors, first-run setup, upgrades, and recovery. ### Docker For always-on servers, the Gateway ships as a public multi-arch image on GHCR: ```bash docker run -d --name kirocrew \ -p 127.0.0.1:5476:5476 \ -v kirocrew-home:/home/kirocrew \ ghcr.io/kirodotdev/kirocrew:stable ``` See the [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md) for first-run login, channel tags, [upgrades](docs/guides/docker.md#state-and-upgrades), and the container security model. ### Build from source macOS and Linux require Python 3.12+, Node.js 22.12+ (24 LTS recommended), and npm. The default ACP backend also requires [`kiro-cli`](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/): install it on the Gateway host and run `kiro-cli login` before using that backend. Other verified ACP harnesses have their own prerequisites in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md). Windows is supported through a native source install; follow the [Windows guide](docs/guides/windows-install.md) instead of the shell steps below. ```bash # 1. Clone and build Kiro Crew git clone https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew.git cd KiroCrew make build source .venv/bin/activate # 2. Configure, verify, and start kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` ## Why Kiro Crew Most agent sessions end when the chat closes. Kiro Crew runs continuously on hardware you control and keeps working between conversations. **Persistent.** Sessions, memory, schedules, and task checkpoints survive Gateway restarts, and scheduled or reactive work continues without someone at the terminal. **Self-learning.** Corrections and task failures become durable lessons. Preferences and project context carry into new sessions. **Self-evolving.** Repeated patterns become reusable skills. Memory, lessons, and skills stay visible and editable, so each Kiro Crew grows more tailored to the person and work around it. **Runs where you choose.** Your Mac, a local container, or a remote machine you control. **One Gateway, many surfaces.** Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue the same work from the CLI and messaging surfaces like Slack and Discord. ## What Kiro Crew does | Capability | What it gives you | |---|---| | **Persistent sessions** | Run concurrent, isolated conversations, resume them after Gateway restarts, search prior sessions, and carry recent context into new work. | | **Self-learning** | Turn corrections and task failures into durable lessons that change later behavior. Lessons can apply globally or carry a `repo_scope` that limits them to one repository; Crew Members keep private lessons in their own memory store. | | **Self-evolving skills** | Synthesize reusable skills from repeated patterns, then inspect, refine, or remove them as your work changes. | | **Long-running tasks** | Give Kiro Crew a task spec and walk away. It plans steps, executes them, validates results, retries failures, and resumes from checkpoints. *"Implement this migration plan and stop if the tests fail"* runs as a checkpointed task with validation at each step. | | **Unattended autonomy** | Run scheduled agent work or deterministic scripts and commands without a model call. Monitor work until it is done, or react to messaging events and authenticated webhooks without someone at the terminal. *"Every weekday at 9, summarize the open work I should review"* becomes a timezone-aware recurring job delivered to the surface you choose. | | **Delegation** | Spawn isolated subagents for parallel work and bring their results back into the parent conversation. *"Research these three options in parallel and recommend one"* fans out to isolated subagents and synthesizes the tradeoffs. | | **Work where you choose** | Work directly in the desktop app or web dashboard, or continue through the CLI and any connected messaging surface without moving the agent runtime or its state. | | **Installable Apps** | Add focused interfaces and domain workflows through dashboard pages, scoped Gateway APIs, events, and lifecycle hooks. | | **Extensible tools** | Add MCP servers, markdown skills, and hooks without changing the core runtime. | | **Visible execution** | Watch tool calls, subagent progress, context usage, approvals, schedules, memory, and logs from the dashboard. | | **Defense in depth** | Combine tool approvals, OS sandboxing, sensitive-path checks, credential redaction, deny rules, audit events, and governance profiles. | You can also paste a screenshot and ask what is causing an error. Kiro Crew sends the image to the active Kiro model and keeps the diagnosis in the conversation history. The complete inventory is in [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md) and [What's New](CHANGELOG.md). ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Desktop app · Web dashboard · CLI · Messaging channels"] G["Gateway
access · sessions · memory · schedules · approvals · apps"] A["Agent sessions
ACP runtime · selected harness · MCP tools · models"] S --> G --> A ``` The Gateway separates where the agent runs from where you work. Each conversation or background task is a logical agent session driven through the selected `agent.acp_backend`; depending on that harness and workload, the session uses a dedicated process or a handle on a shared ACP runtime. State, policy, approvals, schedules, memory, and apps remain on the Gateway host. See the [architecture overview](docs/architecture/overview.md) for component boundaries, [sessions](docs/system-specs/modules/session.md) for lifecycle and isolation, and [MCP architecture](docs/architecture/mcp.md) for tool exposure. ## Security and control Kiro Crew enforces approvals, OS isolation where available, sensitive-path and credential guards, denied-operation rules, audit records, and an optional policy/profile ceiling at the runtime boundary. The dashboard binds to loopback by default; any remote exposure requires authenticated configuration. Read the canonical [security model](docs/system-specs/modules/security.md) and [security architecture](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md) before changing or widening those controls. Protect credentials, review high-impact actions, and use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for private vulnerability reporting. ## Install, configure, and operate The [install guide](docs/guides/install.md) owns every install path, first-run step, optional dependency, upgrade, uninstall, and recovery procedure. User data lives under `~/.kiro/crew` by default and moves with `KIROCREW_HOME`, except some [folders that stay under `~/.kiro`](docs/guides/install.md#folders-beside-the-data-home); configuration keys and precedence are canonical in the [config spec](docs/system-specs/modules/config.md). For a new source or wheel install: ```bash kirocrew setup kirocrew doctor kirocrew gateway ``` Run the Gateway as a boot-persistent service when needed: ```bash kirocrew service install kirocrew service status kirocrew logs ``` Service ports, systemd/launchd behavior, containers, and remote-host access are documented in the [install guide](docs/guides/install.md#running-as-a-service), [Docker guide](docs/guides/docker.md), and [remote host guide](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md). Use `kirocrew config get`, `kirocrew config set `, and `kirocrew config edit` for the main configuration. Set a process port with `KIROCREW_PORT` or `kirocrew gateway --port `. Start troubleshooting with `kirocrew doctor`, then inspect `kirocrew logs` (or `kirocrew logs -f`). See the [troubleshooting guide](src/kiro_crew/docs/troubleshooting.md) for log sources, levels, diagnostics bundles, and recovery steps. ## Anonymous usage telemetry Kiro Crew sends **one anonymous heartbeat per day** so maintainers can see how many copies are actively running and which releases, Python minors, and install paths still need support. After a successful install or update from the official app catalog, it also sends one anonymous per-app receipt. Both signals are enabled by default, but first egress waits until the first-run privacy disclosure has been shown; they use the same controls below. To turn it off, click **Turn off** on the Privacy screen of first-run onboarding, or flip **Settings > Privacy > Send anonymous usage heartbeat** in the dashboard. Or from a terminal: ```bash kirocrew telemetry disable # local metrics and the heartbeat; persists to config.json export KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 # heartbeat only, per-shell / per-container export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 # everything: local metrics and the heartbeat kirocrew telemetry status # print both switches and exactly what would be sent ``` Turn off and `kirocrew telemetry disable` write the same settings, so either one sticks across restarts and upgrades. `KIROCREW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` and `DO_NOT_TRACK` override them: when one is set, the dashboard toggle is disabled and says so. An existing install that turned the heartbeat off, wrote `telemetry.enabled: false`, or sets `DO_NOT_TRACK` keeps local recording off after an upgrade and is not asked again, with one exception. Builds before recording was on by default wrote `telemetry.enabled: false` into every new config. The written value looks the same whether the old build or the person wrote it, so an install whose only reason for being off is a written `telemetry.enabled: false` sees the Privacy screen once, even if the person chose that value. It is an off form that names Kiro telemetry and offers Turn on performance metrics or Keep off. Until you turn them on, only the daily heartbeat and official app install receipts are sent, and no performance metrics are recorded. A terminal-only install gets one line pointing at `kirocrew telemetry enable` instead. When the Privacy screen's text changes, existing users see it once more at their next dashboard load while local recording is on. **Exactly these five fields are sent, at most once per day, and nothing else:** | Field | Example | Why | |-------|---------|-----| | Random instance id | `9c75560d…` (UUID4) | Lets us count how many copies ran on a given day. Generated once on first run and derived from nothing — not your hostname, username, MAC, IP, or any account. It identifies an installed copy, never a person. | | App version | `0.1.2` | Which releases are still in use. **Release number only** — build stamps like `-nightly.20260731t065756` are stripped before sending, because a per-build timestamp is near-unique and would help identify a specific machine. | | Python minor version | `3.12` | When the minimum can move up | | Install path | `dmg` | Which distribution format people actually use | | First-send flag | `1` / `0` | First successfully reported install vs returning | **Official-app install receipts are separate and event-based.** After a successful official-catalog install or update, Kiro Crew sends one GET to `/b/1/install/?t=&k=&v=` on the same telemetry host. The slug is the public catalog identifier. `t` is the first 32 hex characters of HMAC-SHA256 keyed by an independent local receipt secret over `app-install:`; that secret never leaves the machine, so tokens for different apps cannot be linked to each other or to the heartbeat install id. `k` separates fresh installs from updates, and `v` is the same release-only Kiro Crew version clamp used by the heartbeat. Receipts are emitted only for bundled or edition-provided official catalog entries. Apps from user-configured registries, local-directory installs, and self-registered apps emit nothing, so private app names never leave the machine. If the receipt-only secret cannot be persisted, the receipt is skipped. This list used to be nine fields. Release channel, OS, CPU architecture and governance posture were **removed** — each was coarse on its own, but the instance id is stable, so those attributes all describe the *same* copy and together they narrowed the group any one install blends into far more than any single field suggests. We report this as **Daily Active Crews** rather than "users": Kiro Crew has no account system of its own, and the Kiro sign-in that `kiro-cli` uses for model access is never read or sent. There is no way to resolve a copy to a person, so one person running Kiro Crew on three machines counts as three Crews. **Never sent:** your prompts, model responses, file contents, file paths, repo or branch names, credentials, environment variables, hostname, username, or IP address. The receiving CDN is configured **not to log client IP addresses** — the log delivery does not include that field, so no IP is stored at all. **Automatically off** in CI, and whenever `KIROCREW_HOME` points somewhere other than `~/.kiro/crew` (dev instances and pods are never counted). **Enterprise administrators can pin it off entirely.** A `capabilities.telemetry` entry in the security policy blocks both outbound signals regardless of the local setting, and the dashboard toggle then says so instead of offering a change that would not take effect: ```json {"version": 1, "boot": {"fail_closed": true}, "capabilities": {"telemetry": {"enabled": false}}} ``` See [docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md](docs/system-specs/modules/governance.md). This is separate from `telemetry.enabled`, which controls performance metrics. They are on by default, are recorded on your machine, are capped at 30 days and 100 MB, and turn off with the same Turn off button, `kirocrew telemetry disable`, `KIROCREW_TELEMETRY=0` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`. A terminal-only install prints a one-line notice about them on its first start. While they are on, the public build also sends the reviewed product usage metrics (which features are used and how long things take; no prompts, files, paths or credentials) to Kiro telemetry, labelled with a hashed install ID. Nothing is sent until the Privacy screen, or the one-line terminal notice, has named it. It is not sent from an enterprise (LTS) build or a CI runner, and every off switch above stops it. See [docs/guides/telemetry-otlp-export.md](docs/guides/telemetry-otlp-export.md#the-kiro-telemetry-destination) and [docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md](docs/system-specs/modules/metrics.md). ## Docs and contributing | Topic | Start here | |---|---| | Install and packaging | [Install and build](docs/guides/install.md), [Windows](docs/guides/windows-install.md), [Docker](docs/guides/docker.md), [Desktop](docs/build/desktop-app.md), [Remote host](docs/guides/remote-and-mobile.md), [Release process](docs/build/release.md) | | Product capabilities | [Features](src/kiro_crew/docs/index.md), [Skills](skills/README.md), [All user docs](src/kiro_crew/docs/README.md) | | All documentation | [docs/](docs/README.md) for contributor and architecture docs | | Channels | [Slack](docs/guides/slack-setup.md), [Discord](src/kiro_crew/docs/discord-integration.md), [Telegram](src/kiro_crew/docs/telegram-integration.md), [Teams](src/kiro_crew/docs/teams-integration.md), [Webex](src/kiro_crew/docs/webex-integration.md), [WeCom](src/kiro_crew/docs/wecom-integration.md), [WeChat (Weixin)](src/kiro_crew/docs/weixin-integration.md), [WhatsApp](src/kiro_crew/docs/whatsapp-integration.md), [Feishu (Lark)](src/kiro_crew/docs/feishu-integration.md), [iMessage](src/kiro_crew/docs/imessage-integration.md) | | Architecture | [System architecture](docs/architecture/overview.md), [Memory](docs/system-specs/modules/memory-skills-hooks.md), [MCP](docs/architecture/mcp.md), [App Kit](docs/app-kit/getting-started.md) | | Trust and dependencies | [Security](docs/architecture/security-deep-dive.md), [Security policy](SECURITY.md) | | Project work | [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), [Tenets](TENETS.md), [Governance](GOVERNANCE.md), [Maintainers](MAINTAINERS.md), [AI assistant rules](AGENTS.md), [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) | Contributions are welcome. Follow [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup, change-scoped validation, commit format, and the pull-request workflow. Use [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/issues) for bugs and feature requests; report vulnerabilities privately through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Contributors Kiro Crew was made possible by its internal community, the people who supported the project and shipped its code, together with everyone who has since opened a pull request in the open. items.name: cherry-studio-app
items.description: 🍒 This is the mobile version of Cherry Studio.
items.readme_text:
Cherry Studio Mobile

Your AI workspace on iOS and Android.
Chat with your favorite models, connect your tools, and turn ideas into images.

Features · Development · Documentation · Feedback · Desktop

## A Look Inside

Conversations · Image creation · Connected tools
Real app screenshots captured on iPhone 17 Pro.

## Features ### 💬 Your Models, One Conversation Space Connect multiple AI providers, manage your models, and choose the right one for each conversation. Read streaming responses with Markdown formatting and bring images and text attachments into the conversation, subject to the selected model's capabilities. ### 🍒 Agents That Work Your Way Create agents with their own instructions, default models, and tools. Keep separate conversations for different projects, and review tool actions when approval is required. ### 🔌 Connect Your Tools Extend your agents with plugins and MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. Search the web and read pages with configured search services. Connected tools become available according to their setup, permissions, and each agent's configuration. ### 🎨 Turn Ideas Into Images Start from a prompt or a visual template, choose an image model, and create something new. Revisit your drawing history and use existing images as the starting point for another creation. ### 📎 Keep And Share Your Work Manage attachments and generated files in the file library. Preview documents and export selected conversation content as Markdown, HTML, or an image, with available formats depending on the selection. ### 📱 Made For Mobile, Connected To Cherry Use light and dark themes, native navigation, and the system share sheet. Pair with Cherry Studio Desktop to import supported provider configurations and models. Conversation history and remote agent control are outside the current pairing feature. Model and connected-service availability depends on your configuration. Some providers require an account or API key and may charge for usage. ## Development Built with Expo and React Native. Use **Node.js 24** and **pnpm 12.2.1**. ```bash pnpm install # Build and install the development client for one platform: pnpm ios # or: pnpm android # Start Metro for an already installed development client: pnpm dev ``` The app includes custom native modules and requires a development client. See the [development guide](docs/guides/development.md) for setup and daily development, and [Local EAS Builds](docs/guides/local-builds.md) for installation packages and app variants. ## Contributing Help shape Cherry Mobile through code, bug reports, product ideas, and documentation. - [Report a bug or suggest a feature](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio-app/issues/new/choose) - Read the [Git workflow](docs/guides/git-workflow.md) and [testing guide](docs/guides/testing-and-ci.md) before preparing a pull request. - Explore the [project documentation](docs/README.md) for architecture and development conventions. ## Community Cherry Mobile is part of [Cherry Studio](https://github.com/CherryHQ/cherry-studio). [Official website](https://cherry-ai.com) · [Discord](https://discord.gg/wez8HtpxqQ) · [Telegram](https://t.me/CherryStudioAI) ## License [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0](LICENSE).
